## Pre-race

This felt like a return race more than anything else.

Three weeks earlier I was in ER with chest pain, and three days earlier I
started blood pressure medication. For a while it was not even clear whether I
would make it to this start -or the finish- line at all.

The doctor said that, even if there was no sign of heart issues, it was
probably a good idea to skip this one given how recently I had started the medication.
I decided to race anyway. The obvious disclaimer applies here: don't be like me;
if your doctor tells you not to race, listen.

The main reason I was willing to take the risk was that this was a duathlon,
not a triathlon. No swim. That matters, because swimming is notoriously where the vast majority
of heart-related accidents happen. On the bike or the run,
if I had felt anything concerning, I could simply have stopped and gotten
assistance on land.

Before even thinking about performance, the first objective was just to get to
the line and finish safely.

## A Tough Build-up

I knew I was not ready for a good race.

Between the ER visit and the mandatory period of taking things easy
afterwards, I had missed exactly the kind of high-end work that gives you
that sharp edge you need to be competitive. I was not coming into this race
with the feeling that I could really push the top end. At best, I hoped I
could manage the effort.

Then, during race week, I found out this event was also the Ontario Provincial
Championship for sprint duathlon. That was not ideal news for a supposedly "easy" return race.
It meant the field was likely to be deeper and harder than usual.

On top of that, I started taper week feeling completely drained. On Monday my
Garmin training readiness was `1/100`, which is as low as it goes. That confirmed
pretty clearly that the body was not in a great place.

So the priority in the final days was simple: recovery first. I kept things
easy, took single easy days seriously, and tried to arrive at the race feeling
less depleted than I had at the start of the week. I did manage to recover
enough that by race morning I felt functional again, which at that point was a
meaningful win on its own.

## Race morning

During the warm-up I actually felt OK.

Sure, I was getting out of breath easily, but I was expecting that. Still, I felt
reasonably well.
Not fitter, but a bit more settled. Given everything that had happened in the
previous few weeks, that was enough to give me some confidence that I could at
least get through the day.

## Run 1

I started the first run with the usual intention of controlling myself, and
with the usual outcome of not really controlling myself at all.

The target was around `4:20/km`. Instead, I went out at about `4:05/km`. That
is just classic race-day stupidity from me at this point. Still, early on I
felt OK. I was working, but not in a way that immediately felt destructive.

The only athletes I could really see ahead of me at first looked older, which
was a slightly mixed feeling. Not great for the overall race, but at least
they did not look like direct competition for my age group.

By the second lap, though, the lack of fitness started to come through. The
pace drifted out beyond `4:20/km`, and that was when a couple of guys from my
age group came past me. Not surprising, but still a clear reminder that I was
racing without the engine I would normally want for this kind of event.

### Performance review

Let's dive a bit deeper into the numbers. Below is a graph of some key metrics over time.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

activities_metadata <- read.csv(
  "analysis_data/activities_metadata.csv",
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

activities_data <- read.csv(
  "analysis_data/activities_data.csv",
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  na.strings = c("NA", "")
)

run_1_id <- activities_metadata |>
  filter(EVENT_TYPE == "RUN") |>
  distinct(ID) |>
  slice(1) |>
  pull(ID)

run_1_plot_data <- activities_data |>
  filter(ID == run_1_id) |>
  transmute(
    time_min = as.numeric(SECS) / 60,
    pace_min_km = as.numeric(PACE),
    power_w = na_if(as.numeric(WATTS), 0),
    cadence_spm = na_if(as.numeric(CAD), 0),
    hr_bpm = na_if(as.numeric(HR), 0)
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(pace_min_km, power_w, cadence_spm, hr_bpm),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    metric = factor(
      metric,
      levels = c("pace_min_km", "power_w", "cadence_spm", "hr_bpm"),
      labels = c("Pace [min/km]", "Power [W]", "Cadence [spm]", "HR [bpm]")
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(value))

format_pace <- function(pace_min_km) {
  total_seconds <- round(pace_min_km * 60)
  minutes <- total_seconds %/% 60
  seconds <- total_seconds %% 60
  sprintf("%d:%02d/km", minutes, seconds)
}

run_1_average_table <- run_1_plot_data |>
  mutate(
    period = case_when(
      time_min >= 5 & time_min < 14 ~ "Before breaking point",
      time_min >= 14 ~ "After breaking point",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(period)) |>
  group_by(metric, period) |>
  summarise(value = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(
    value = case_when(
      metric == "Pace [min/km]" ~ format_pace(value),
      TRUE ~ as.character(round(value))
    )
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = value) |>
  select(metric, `Before breaking point`, `After breaking point`) |>
  rename(Metric = metric)

ggplot(run_1_plot_data, aes(x = time_min, y = value)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5, color = "#1f4e79") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 14, color = "red", linewidth = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Time [min]",
    y = NULL,
    title = "Run 1 performance review"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

I highlighted the breaking point with a red line. At around minute 14 my lack of fitness
started to show. The cadence in particular exposes it mechanically. Fatigue sets in and I cannot
keep the leg going anymore.

Let's see how these metrics dropped before and after the breaking point.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

knitr::kable(run_1_average_table, align = c("l", "r", "r"))
```

Cadence and power dropped significantly, and as a consequence so did the pace. HR stayed
relatively consistent. Not sure if that is a good sign (it did not give up) or a bad sign
(I slowed down but still it stayed high).

```{r}

#| warning: false

top_run_1_men_40_49 <- read.csv(
```

## Bike

Then onto the bike, where of course I immediately messed up the tech.

I forgot to press the transition button, so part of the ride ended up being
recorded as transition. Not ideal, but also very on brand.

Still, the actual riding felt good.

I was keeping things under control and riding mostly by feel rather than by
chasing power numbers -of course I did not even have power numbers since my watch thought
I was still in transition for half the ride...-. The idea was to sit at an effort that felt strong but
not reckless, something that would not completely destroy the legs before the
final run. For that kind of controlled ride, it actually went fairly well. I
was moving through the field and passing people, including one of the
athletes in my age group who had gone by me on the first run.

Looking at the data afterwards, it was not an especially fast ride. On a very
flat course like this, I know I can ride faster on a better day. But given the
interrupted build-up, the medication change, and the basic goal of just
getting through the race safely, it was an OK outcome.

The more important issue came late in the bike leg, when the first real red
flags of the day started to appear. Not cardiovascular red flags, thankfully,
but cramps. Both lower legs started to threaten, which is never a great sign
when you still have another run to do.

### Performance review

Because the watch stayed in transition for the start of the ride, the bike file
does not begin at the true start of the bike leg. I joined T1 and bike data to get
a fuller picture, but while that will give me speed and HR, it will not give me power
or cadence for the whole ride.


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(jsonlite)

activities_metadata <- read.csv(
  "analysis_data/activities_metadata.csv",
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

activities_data <- read.csv(
  "analysis_data/activities_data.csv",
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  na.strings = c("NA", "")
)

bike_id <- activities_metadata |>
  filter(EVENT_TYPE == "BIKE") |>
  distinct(ID) |>
  slice(1) |>
  pull(ID)

t1_json_text <- readLines(
  file("analysis_data/2026_08_09_08_21_18.json", encoding = "UTF-8-BOM"),
  warn = FALSE
)

t1_raw_samples <- fromJSON(paste(t1_json_text, collapse = "\n"))$RIDE$SAMPLES |>
  as_tibble() |>
  transmute(
    time_min = as.numeric(SECS) / 60,
    speed_kph = as.numeric(KPH),
    power_w = NA_real_,
    hr_bpm = na_if(as.numeric(HR), 0)
  )

t1_duration_seconds <- max(t1_raw_samples$time_min, na.rm = TRUE) * 60

bike_raw_data <- activities_data |>
  filter(ID == bike_id) |>
  transmute(
    time_min = (as.numeric(SECS) + t1_duration_seconds) / 60,
    speed_kph = as.numeric(KPH),
    power_w = na_if(as.numeric(WATTS), 0),
    hr_bpm = na_if(as.numeric(HR), 0)
  ) |>
  filter(time_min > max(t1_raw_samples$time_min, na.rm = TRUE))

bike_plot_data <- bind_rows(t1_raw_samples, bike_raw_data) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(speed_kph, power_w, hr_bpm),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    metric = factor(
      metric,
      levels = c("speed_kph", "power_w", "hr_bpm"),
      labels = c("Speed [km/h]", "Power [W]", "HR [bpm]")
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(value))

bike_average_table <- bike_plot_data |>
  group_by(metric) |>
  summarise(Average = round(mean(value, na.rm = TRUE)), .groups = "drop") |>
  rename(Metric = metric)

ggplot(bike_plot_data, aes(x = time_min, y = value)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5, color = "#1f4e79") +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Time since T1 start [min]",
    y = NULL,
    title = "Bike performance review"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

The data is telling us that it was a very even ride. Not too hard,
as the HR went down from the run, and pretty consistent. If only I could run in the
same way...
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

knitr::kable(bike_average_table, align = c("l", "r"))
```

```{r}

top_bike_men_40_49 <- read.csv(
```

I did not know it at the time, but at this point I was running out of T2 in
first place with 40s on Andrew Roberts. Would that be enough? 

## Run 2

I did get out onto the second run, but from the first steps it was obvious
that this was no longer about racing hard.

I had to keep the effort very controlled because even a small increase seemed
to trigger cramps. And it was not just the calves. I was getting cramping in
both lower and upper legs, and even between the shoulders.

So the final run became an exercise in damage limitation. Keep moving, stay
just below the point where everything locks up, and get to the finish line
without the whole thing turning into a shuffle.

With about `500m` to go, one guy in my age group came past me. Part of me
wanted to go with him, just to see if I could hold on. But I was too aware of
what the legs were threatening to do. Chasing him might have meant blowing up
completely, and that did not feel worth it on a day like this. On top of that,
his calf nuber was 46: he was in my age group for the race, but not for the 
qualification spot at the World Championship.

So I let him go and focused on bringing it home cleanly.


### Performance review

And here is how the second run went down.

```{r}
format_pace <- function(pace_min_km) {

ggplot(run_2_plot_data, aes(x = time_min, y = value)) +

  labs(
    x = "Time [min]",
```

This time there was no clear breaking point. It was just a slow run. The cadence slowly
dropped, but not too much. The legs were just heavy.

## Results

And then, finally, the finish line.

I was not expecting much from this race, so ending up `2nd` in category felt
better than I had any real right to expect. It was a bit bittersweet, because
I do think that on a better day I could probably have won this one.

Considering everything that happened in the lead-in to this race, I happily take this result.

This race was also the last World Championship qualifier of the year, which
adds another layer to it. 

Maybe this was enough to secure the spot, if I had not already done enough
earlier in the season. But qualification is never that simple. There were five
guys in the `30-39` range who were faster than me, and if any of them submitted an EOI
and age into `40-44` next year, they would move ahead in the official
federation ranking. So for now it is still a waiting game. We should know more
in the next few weeks.

There is also the season ranking side of it. This result should put me `2nd`
in the Multisport Canada duathlon standings, level on points with the guy who
finished ahead of me today, and `25` points behind the leader, who now has two
wins from two races. So there is still a realistic chance of finishing the
season in the top three.
